list.listitem: Suspect hypocalcemia when at risk patients present with tetany, extra-pyramidal symptoms, seizures, change in mental status, prolonged QT interval in ECG, hypomagnesemia, unexplained skin or dental abnormalities. Most mild hypocalcemias are asymptomatic. C
Diagnose hypocalcemia when the calcium concentration is below 8.5 mg/dL and the ionized serum calcium concentration is below 1.1 mmol/L.

Acute severe symptomatic hypocalcemia should be treated with IV calcium gluconate 1 to 2 grams (100-200 elemental calcium) over 10 to 20 minutes and 4 grams over 4 hours. This is followed by slow infusion of IV calcium gluconate or chloride. C
Mild asymptomatic hypocalcemia and chronic hypocalcemia can be treated with oral calcium with or without vitamin D. C

Vitamin D deficient patients should be given both calcium and vitamin D. Calcium with vitamin D (each containing 400 IU) given daily and in severe vitamin D deficiency higher doses of vitamin such as 50 000 IU oral once a week or 300 000 IU intra muscular every 3 months given. C

background.definition: Hypocalcemia is defined as a calcium concentration below 8.5 mg/dL(normal calcium is 8.5-10.5 mg/dL/OR 2.1-2.6 mmol/L). As ionized calcium is the active form of calcium in the blood, clinically significant hypocalcemia occurs when ionized serum calcium concentration is below 1.1 mmol/L (1.1-1.3 mmol/L, 4.4-5.2 mg/dL).

list.listitem: Hypocalcemia can occur up to 80% to 90% of the ICU patients. Hypocalcemia is associated with increased mortality in ICU patients.

Causes for hypocalcemia can be categorized into low calcium intake/absorption, defective metabolism and increased urinary excretion of calcium. It can also be categorized based on the serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) level.
Hypocalcemia in children is commonly due to congenital anomaly in the metabolism, hypoparathyroidism and vitamin D deficiency and in adults secondary causes are more common.
Renal failure causes hypocalcemia due to hyperphosphatemia and impairment of synthesis of active form of vitamin D.

Hypoparathyroidism, hereditary and acquired, is a cause of hypocalcemia. Hereditary hypoparathyroidism is rare and often associated with other congenital abnormalities. In children, causes include dysfunctional or idiopathic hypoparathyroidism or congenital).

Acquired hypoparathyroidism in adults occurs most commonly after neck surgery involving thyroid gland, parathyroid gland, radiation to the neck, infiltrative disease of the thyroid or parathyroid glands.
Hypocalcemia in patients with normal or high levels of PTH can occur due to pseudohypoparathyroidism i.e., PTH receptor abnormality.

Vitamin D deficiency cases hypocalcemia in people who have low exposure to ultraviolet light especially if the dietary intake vitamin D is low. Decrease vitamin D intake, defect in vitamin D metabolism in the liver and kidney or calcium sensing receptor abnormality.
Severe hypomagnesemia (<0.4 mmol/L; <0.8 meq/L) causes hypocalcemia by decreasing PTH secretion or end organ response.
In critically ill patients hypocalcemia occurs due to impaired PTH secretion or action, impaired vitamin D synthesis or action, or calcium chelation/precipitation.
Hypocalcemia is common in shocked trauma patients.

Loss of calcium from extracellular fluid and other multiple mechanisms cause hypocalcemia in acute pancreatitis, osteoblastic metastasis, low phosphate, increased citrate and acetate in the blood and respiratory alkalosis. Tumor lysis syndrome causes hypocalcemia secondary to hyperphosphatemia.
Other causes include fluoride intoxication, hypercalciuria, malabsorption (e.g., celiac disease), small bowel resection or disease, hyperoxaluria, magnesium sulfate infusion, and HIV disease.
Transient hypocalcemia is seen in severe sepsis, burns, acute renal failure, and extensive transfusions with citrated blood.
Medication induced hypocalcemia can occur with bisphosphonate protamine, heparin and glucagon, anticonvulsant treatment with dilantin or barbiturates, zoledronic acid etc.
Gadolinium based contrast can cause falsely lower calcium in the blood.

99% of total body calcium is located in the bones. Ionized calcium, representing 50% of the total serum calcium, is the active form. Approximately 40% of serum calcium is protein bound and 10% is chelated. Serum pH influences calcium binding to albumin hence the level of ionized calcium. Ionized calcium and inorganic phosphate are under hormonal control.

Main regulators of calcium metabolism are PTH, the active form of vitamin D (calcitriol) and thyrocalcitonin. In patients with certain malignancies PTH related peptide also plays a role in calcium metabolism.
Net calcium absorption in the intestine is 10% to 20% of ingested calcium level.

In response to decreased serum calcium, increased PTH secretion leads to increase tubular re-absorption of calcium in the kidneys, resorption of calcium from bones and increased 1,25(OH) 2D productions. 1,25(OH) 2D acts principally on the intestine to increase calcium absorption to increase the calcium level in the blood.
Any defect on any of the above mechanisms can cause hypocalcemia.
Suspect hypocalcemia in patients presenting with tetany, seizures, extrapyramidal and neuro-psychiatric symptoms, and dental, ocular or bone abnormalities. Hypocalcemia can also be asymptomatic. C
Hypocalcemia is present when the corrected serum calcium level is <8.5 mg/dL and the ionized serum calcium (active form) concentration is <1.1 mmol/L. C

Initial laboratory evaluation should include serum phosphorus, PTH measured simultaneously with serum and ionized calcium, vitamin D (calcidiol and calcitriol), serum magnesium, serum creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase. If significant hypocalcemia or symptomatic obtain ECG. C
Low PTH level suggests hypoparathyroidism and high or normal level of PTH suggests pseudohypoparathyroidism. C
Low Vitamin D, hypophosphatemia and high PTH level signifies Vitamin D deficiency as the cause of hypocalcemia. C

Differential.Differential_Features: High phosphorus, normal or high parathyroid hormone
Normal phosphorus, low or high parathyroid hormone
High phosphorus, high parathyroid hormone, low calcitriol (1,25(OH)2D)
Low phosphorus, high parathyroid hormone, high alkaline phosphatase

list.listitem: Symptoms are caused by increased excitability in the neuromuscular junctions and or deposition of calcium in tissues. The major determinants of symptom severity are the level of ionized calcium, how rapidly calcium declines, and the duration of hypocalcemia. Acute hypocalcemia can present with tetany, seizures, extrapyramidal symptoms and even coma. Sometimes symptoms of acute hypocalcemia are masked due to an underlying acute condition.

Tetany: May presents with paresthesia in the fingers around the mouth and carpopedal spasms; can be elicited by Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs (more specific) in high risk individuals. Infants with symptomatic hypocalcemia can presents with Swan neck sign of the big toe (big toe hyperextended and metatarsophalangeal joint and flexed interphalangeal joint).
Other neuromuscular symptoms: confusion/change in mental status, movement disorder, psychiatric manifestations and myopathy.
Cardiac manifestations: arrhythmias and rarely myocardial dysfunction.

Chronic hypocalcemia is usually asymptomatic but sometimes causes mild symptoms over a period of time. Chronic symptomatic hypocalcemia may present as rickets in children. Other neurological signs such as extrapyramidal symptoms, basal ganglia calcification can occur in chronic hypocalcemia.

Other manifestations of chronic hypocalcemia: dry and puffy skin, brittle, coarse and sparse hair and dental abnormalities such as hypoplasia, failure of tooth eruption and defective enamel and abnormalities in root formation. Early cataract formation and papilledema are ophthalmologic manifestations. Endocrine manifestations like low insulin, prolactin, and premature ovarian failure can occur with autoimmune hypoparathyroidism.

Clinical features suggesting underlying causes of hypocalcemia include gastrointestinal steatorrhea, celiac disease, skeletal abnormalities, rickets and osteomalacia (decrease dietary intake of calcium) and increase bone mineral density or osteosclerosis.

Hypoparathyroidism and pseudohypoparathyroidism usually presents in adolescents and in adults as chronic hypocalcemia. Secondary causes include renal failure, vitamin D deficiency or defect in calcium metabolism. Patients with severe alcohol intake may present with magnesium depletion related hypocalcemia.

Measure serum and ionized calcium level when diagnosing hypocalcemia (see ). Initial laboratory evaluation should include serum phosphorus, PTH measured simultaneously with serum and ionized calcium, vitamin D (calcidiol and calcitriol), serum magnesium, serum creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase. Consider 24 hour excretion of calcium in the urine or screening test Ca/Cr ratio.

Simultaneous measurement of serum PTH and calcium is important in hypocalcemic patients. PTH levels are low in hypoparathyroidism, and elevated in other causes of hypocalcemia. Low PTH level suggests hypoparathyroidism (congenital or acquired) as the cause of hypocalcemia. In pseudohypoparathyroidism PTH level may be high or normal. Low phosphorus may indicate vitamin D deficiency or secondary hyperparathyroidism. High phosphorus without renal insufficiency is seen in hypoparathyroidism or pseudohypoparathyroidism.
Chronic renal insufficiency (as measured by an elevated serum creatinine) may be associated with hypocalcemia due to reduction in calcitriol.
Low magnesium levels cause decrease in PTH secretion or end organ resistance causing hypocalcemia.

Vitamin D deficiency causes hypocalcemia which in turn increases PTH secretion by directly and indirectly removing the inhibitory effects of vitamin D (1, 25 (OH) 2) on PTH. Hypophosphatemia is common in vitamin D deficiency. Low 25 (OH) D in the setting of hypocalcemia signifies decreased intake and absorption of vitamin D. Alkaline phosphatase can be abnormal in rickets and adult osteomalacia.

Older age and low preoperative serum 25 OHD level and low postoperative serum PTH level are significantly associated with postoperative hypocalcemia in patients after total thyroidectomy for non toxic multinodular goiter. Single measurement of PTH concentration in the early postoperative period predicts who are likely to develop hypocalcemia. See for diagnosis and management summary algorithm.

Order ECG: cardiac abnormalities include evidence of QT interval prolongation of >450 ms, ventricular arrhythmias, and flattened T waves. Conversely, one study failed to identify any electrolyte abnormality (including hypocalcemia) in 258 consecutive patients admitted with a prolonged QT interval. If evidence of heart failure consider echocardiogram.
Confirm hypocalcemia by obtaining an ionized calcium (<1.1 mmol/L). See for correction formulas.

Look for causes of hypocalcemia: a history of neck surgery, signs and symptoms of renal failure, vitamin or nutritional deficiencies, acute pancreatitis, cell lysis syndrome, medications, severe alcohol intake.

Initial laboratory evaluation should include serum phosphorus, PTH measured simultaneously with serum and ionized calcium, vitamin D (calcidiol and calcitriol), serum magnesium, serum creatinine, and alkaline phosphatase. If significant hypocalcemia or symptomatic obtain ECG and consider amylase, lipase, and 24 hour excretion of calcium in the urine or screening test Ca/Cr ratio.
See for summary of diagnostic and treatment algorithm.
Treat acute severe hypocalcemia with IV calcium under monitored conditions. C
Give IV magnesium for acute severe symptomatic hypocalcemia in patients with known hypomagnesemia or unknown magnesium level but normal renal function. C
Treat chronic and acute mild symptomatic or asymptomatic hypocalcemia with oral calcium with vitamin D if necessary. C

Vitamin D deficient patients should be given both calcium and vitamin D. A minimum of 400 to 800 IU should be given daily and in severe vitamin D deficiency higher doses of vitamin such as 50 000 IU oral once a week or 300 000 IU intra muscular every 3 months may be required. C

Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is treated with IV calcium gluconate 2 grams (100-200 elemental calcium) over 10 to 20 minutes. Patients must be monitored for cardiac arrhythmias, especially during the initial rapid phase of replacement. When ionized calcium is 1 to 1.2 mmol/l, give calcium gluconate 2 grams in 50 to 150 ml over 2 hours; if ionized calcium is less than 1 mmol/l, give 4 g of calcium gluconate in 50 to 150 ml over 4 hours. This is followed by slow IV infusion with 10% calcium gluconate or 10% calcium chloride usually diluted with dextrose at 0.5 to 2.0 mg/kg/hour. Calcium infusions are not given in saline (increases urinary excretion) or with bicarbonate or phosphate (deposits in tissues). IV treatment should continue until patient is stable and can take oral supplements.
Avoid calcium chloride as it is an irritant. Extravasation of calcium chloride as well as calcium gluconate causes tissue necrosis.

Treat the underlying condition while treating for hypocalcemia and monitor serial serum calcium levels in all the patients who get calcium supplements (e.g., every 4-6 hours in severe symptomatic hypocalcemia).
Magnesium should be repleted in addition to calcium in patients with hypomagnesemia and in an emergency, patients with normal renal function and unknown magnesium level.

Mild, asymptomatic hypocalcemia and chronic hypocalcemia: treat with oral calcium 1000 to 2600 mg daily, in divided doses 3-4 times taken between meals. Different oral calcium preparations have varying amount of elemental calcium, calcium carbonate (250), calcium citrate (200), calcium gluconate (90) and calcium lactate (60). Calcium carbonate is cheap but absorption is limited in achlorhydria. Vitamin D is usually given with oral calcium. Combined calcium and vitamin D are preferred preparations.

Hypoparathyroidism and psudohypoparathyroidism: Treat with both vitamin D preparation and high dose of oral calcium. Vitamin D 40,000 to 120,000 U/d (1-3 mg/d) and more than 1 g of elemental calcium are given. Calcitriol or alfacalcidol is needed and starting doses are 0.5 Mg (microgram) of calcitriol or 1 Mg (microgram) alfa-calcidiol daily while increasing the dose to keep the calcium in the normal range.

Renal failure: symptomatic hypocalcemia should to be treated with phosphate binders to lower the phosphate concentration. Calcium carbonate is commonly used. A higher dose of vitamin D or calcitriol is also used in renal failure patients.

Vitamin D deficiency: give both calcium and vitamin D. Most available vitamin D contains calcium in it. Most combined calcium with vitamin D preparations contain 500 or 600 mg calcium and 100- or 200 IU of D. A minimum of 400-800 IU should be given daily and in severe vitamin D deficiency higher doses of vitamin such as 50 000 IU oral once a week or 300 000 IU intra muscular every 3 months may be required. It has shown Vitamin D supplementation was superior to sun light in girls (11-15 y) with hypovitaminosis D without any evidence of rickets. When getting treated with vitamin D and calcium it is useful to check the urine calcium to prevent hypercalciuria, i.e., marker of excess vitamin D.
Give hydrochlorothiazide to patients with osteopenia and inadequate response to dietary modification in the setting of hypercalciuria because of its ability to lower urinary calcium excretion.

Thyroidectomy: oral calcium and vitamin D prevent symptoms of hypocalcemia in patients undergoing a total thyroidectomy. Early and combined oral calcium and vitamin D is better at preventing post operative hypocalcemia than only oral calcium. Calcitriol and hydrochlorothiazide have been used prevent transient post thyroidectomy hypocalcemia.
Plasma exchange: continuous infusion of calcium gluconate in 5% albumin prevents hypocalcemic reactions occur with plasma exchange.
See for diagnostic and treatment algorithm.
Some of the calcium rich foods include green leafy vegetables such as kale, small bony fish and seaweed.
Dairy products like milk, yoghurt and cheese are high in calcium but also high in PO4. Most of the commercially available cereals and juices are fortified with calcium and vitamin D.
Vitamin D rich foods include fatty fish and plants.
Any symptomatic hypocalcemia needs hospitalization for treatment and to investigate the etiology.
Asymptomatic unexplained hypocalcemic patients may need to be referred to an endocrinologist.
Pregnant hypoparathyroid patients require close and frequent monitoring of serum calcium as calcium requirement increases significantly throughout the pregnancy.
Calcium requirement after the delivery is calculated based on the lactation status.
Early neonatal period hypocalcemia may occur due to underdeveloped parathyroid gland (i.e., Di George Syndrome).
Hypocalcemia and hypocalcemic seizures have been seen in infants with rickets.
In neonates gestational age and bodyweight also have to be taken into consideration in calculating serum calcium level.

Based on the severity of symptoms calcium is replaced either as slow IV infusions or as oral supplements. Body weight is taken into consideration when calculating the dose. IV calcium should be given carefully under close cardiac monitoring.

cell.label: Hypocalcemia (Ca <8.5 mg/dl and/or ionized Ca <1.1 mmol/L). Acute and severe symptoms (tetany, seizures, coma, arrhythmia)?
Cardiac monitor, ECG, vital signs, arterial blood gas. Initiate urgent treatment.
Give IV calcium gluconate 1−2 g over 10-20 minutes or 4 g over 4 hours followed by 10% IV calcium gluconate infusion. IV magnesium if indicated, frequent monitoring of calcium level.
Clear etiology (medications, neck surgery, severe sepsis, tumor lysis, pancreatitis, massive transfusion or organ dysfunction)?
Treat the underlying condition while replacing calcium.
History and physical, serum phosphorus, PTH, vitamin D, magnesium, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase. Consider ECG.
Malabsorption (e.g., celiac disease): treat the underlying condition and supplement the losses.
Vitamin D deficiency or resistance: calcium with vitamin D oral or intramuscular in severe and diet with high calcium.
Hypoparathyroidism or pseudohypo-parathyroidism: calcitriol or alfa-calcidol.
Chronic renal failure: Phosphate binders and vitamin D + calcium and dietary modification.
